short: The first state to rule Mesopotamia as a single realm.
full:
Sargon of Akkad, by tradition a cupbearer who seized the throne of Kish, brought the Sumerian city-states under one authority from a capital, Agade, that archaeologists have still not located. Middle-chronology dates put his accession around 2334 BCE. He and his successors, above all his grandson Naram-Sin, campaigned from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean, installed their own governors in conquered cities, and made Akkadian a language of administration alongside Sumerian.

The empire held together for roughly 180 years. Its collapse around 2154 BCE was blamed by later scribes on Gutian incursions from the Zagros mountains; climate evidence points instead to a long drought beginning about 2200 BCE. Either way, the Akkadian template outlived the state. A king styled ruler of the four quarters, a standing army, provincial governors and year-names dated by royal deeds were all reused by Ur III, Babylon and Assyria, and Sargon remained a figure of legend in Mesopotamian writing for two thousand years.
